Which lens is the cloud made of?

Three models were built in May and saved in the bundle. This page plays them so the revival can start from what they sound like. Nothing plays until you click it, one take at a time, and a take stops if you leave the page.

The phrase

Start here, so the ear knows what the clouds are made of.

the phrase, dry
Kokoro reading “the prism, and the cloud.” Every take below is this phrase.

Three answers to “what is the lens?”

Each model is a different answer to what the cloud is made of. The first is a familiar shimmer; the second is a crowd of near-copies; the third is the prism taken literally.

01 · feedback lens
One lens: shift up an octave, delay, feed back, six times over. The classic shimmer tail.
02 · droplet cloud
Hundreds of copies, each played back a hair faster or slower, panned and scattered in time.
03 · dispersion cloud
Hundreds of lenses that keep the pitch and delay each frequency by a different amount.
your ear

Your shimmer, two kinds of physics

In May you asked for “many droplets, very close to in tune, slowly falling out of time, panned wide.” Here it is twice: once by playing copies at slightly different speeds, once by delaying each frequency differently. Same intent, different physics underneath.

A · droplets
600 droplets, ±3 cents, 350 ms spread, full pan.
B · dispersion
600 lenses, 4–20 ms dispersion, 350 ms spread, full pan. No pitch shift.
your ear

What dispersion adds

The same cloud with no dispersion, then with the textbook prism. If the prism is doing anything, this pair is where you'll hear it: listen to the “s” in prism.

A · pure delay
Every frequency delayed the same. No dispersion at all.
B · linear prism
Delay grows with frequency. The textbook prism.
your ear

Pure, or with a little drift

Your canonical dispersion again, against the same thing with the droplets' ±3 cents laid on top. This is the layered model: does the shimmer want both?

B · dispersion
600 lenses, 4–20 ms dispersion, 350 ms spread, full pan. No pitch shift.
B · dispersion + drift
Your canonical dispersion, plus ±3 cents of pitch jitter on every lens.
your ear

What the third lens does

Each dispersing lens leaves the spectrum's loudness alone and turns its phase, more for some frequencies than others:

φ(fₙ) = −direction × (π × D ÷ exponent) × fₙ^exponent(phase turn at frequency n) = −(which way it leans) × (π × (largest delay) ÷ (curve shape)) × (frequency n)^(curve shape)

With a curve shape of 1 every frequency waits the same; at 2 it is the textbook prism. That is the second pair above.
